records.name: Borno
records.current_summary: Borno is one of the twelve northern Nigerian states applying Sharia criminal law in parallel with the federal system since the 1999–2002 wave. A June 2025 government country-of-origin note lists Borno among the states where the Sharia penal code remains in force for Muslims, criminalising same-sex acts between men (death penalty the maximum) and between women (penalties up to flogging and imprisonment), with a dedicated section on enforcement and the religious police — the legal architecture, not a case record, is the finding.  No trans-specific incident, no Hisbah case and no court-level study covers Borno in this dossier; the bloc's own reporting caveat is that enforcement data capture only a fraction of actual cases, so silence is not evidence of safety. The federal criminal code's coverage of men's acts (up to 14 years) applies here as everywhere in Nigeria.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch's 2004 report lists Borno among the twelve northern states that had adopted Shari'a into criminal legislation by 2002, with Shari'a courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslims beyond federal law.

UK Home Office country-of-origin information note (June 2025) on sexual orientation and gender identity in Nigeria: Islamic law applies to Muslims in the 12 northern states and criminalises same-sex sexual acts both between men and between women; the maximum penalty for 'sodomy' for men is death in all 12 states and penalties for 'lesbianism' range from death to flogging and imprisonment; includes a dedicated section on enforcement of Sharia provisions and the attitude of the hisbah (morality police).

Ostien's Volume III reproduces Borno State's own statute on prostitution, homosexuality, brothels and other sexual immoralities (2000), gazetted in Borno State Gazette No. 42 Vol. 26 on 18 October 2001 and signed by Governor Kachalla on 10 December 2000. Section 3 makes engaging in prostitution, lesbianism, a homosexual act or pimping an offence in the State; Section 7 provides that any person who 'engages in sexual intercourse with another person of the same gender shall upon conviction be punished with death'; Section 4 deems all brothels closed on commencement; and Section 9 assigns jurisdiction to the Upper Sharia Courts, Area Courts and Magistrate Courts. Borno's own enacted death penalty for same-gender intercourse independently supports this record's finding that the state's legal architecture, not just the national framework, criminalises same-sex conduct.

The sourcebook's list of enacted Sharia Penal Codes records Borno's Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, signed into law on 3 March 2003, with no operation date or gazette identified; the editor notes the Borno text was obtained only in May 2006, after the volume's annotation had been completed, which is why Borno is not among the individually annotated codes. Confirms Borno enacted its own state Sharia Penal Code legislation in addition to its secular morality law, so the record's claimed parallel Sharia layer for Borno rests on a Borno-specific enactment rather than mere umbrella coverage.

records.name: Jigawa
records.current_summary: Jigawa is among the twelve northern Nigerian states whose Sharia penal codes, adopted in the 1999–2002 wave, give religious courts criminal jurisdiction over Muslims. A June 2025 government country-of-origin note confirms Jigawa's code remains in force, criminalising same-sex sexual acts by men (death the maximum) and by women (flogging and up to six months' imprisonment) — coverage the federal code, which reaches only men's acts, does not supply independently.  No trans-specific incident, Hisbah record or court-level study covers Jigawa in this dossier; like the rest of the bloc its enforcement statistics are acknowledged as partial. The finding is the enacted parallel jurisdiction and its statutory reach over women's conduct.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch report (2004) on the extension of Sharia to criminal law in Nigeria: Zamfara's governor was first, introducing the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999 (in force 27 January 2000), and by 2002 twelve northern states had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation - to date the only states where Sharia courts have jurisdiction to try criminal cases.

The UK Home Office's June 2025 country note carries a twelve-state Sharia penalties table with Jigawa's own row: Sharia Penal Code (2000) — 'Married men: death by stoning,' 'Unmarried men: 100 lashes and imprisonment for up to one year,' and up to 50 lashes with imprisonment for up to 6 months for same-sex acts between women; section 8.2.20 points to the note's Sharia section on the codes in force in Kano, Borno, Kaduna and other northern states. Dated government confirmation that Jigawa's Sharia penal layer remains the operative criminal frame for Muslims in the state, matching this record's June 2025 country-of-origin note claim.

The sourcebook lists Jigawa's Sharia Penal Code Law 2000, Law No. 12 of 2000, signed into law on 18 December 2000 and coming into operation on 27 December 2000 (Jigawa State Gazette Vol. 1 No. 12), and annotates Jigawa among the four states (with Gombe, Kano and Zamfara) whose sodomy offence punishes unmarried men with 100 lashes plus one year's imprisonment and married men with stoning to death (rajm); lesbianism carries up to 50 lashes plus up to six months' imprisonment, with Jigawa including the 'unnatural fusion of the female sexual organs' explanation of the offence. Enactment-level detail for the record's claim that Jigawa's 1999-2002-wave code criminalises acts the federal code does not reach, including women's same-sex conduct.

records.name: Kaduna
records.current_summary: Kaduna carries both layers of criminalisation that define Nigeria's northern bloc. Its 2017 secular Penal Code punishes 'unnatural offences' — covering acts between men and between women — with up to 21 years' imprisonment plus fine; and, per a June 2025 government country-of-origin note, the state's Sharia penal code additionally applies to Muslims through religious courts with criminal jurisdiction, in force since the 1999–2002 wave, with the bloc's capital maximum for men's acts.  No trans-specific incident or documented Hisbah enforcement appears for Kaduna in this dossier, and no court-level study samples it. The finding is the stacked architecture: a long-term secular offence alongside a parallel religious jurisdiction, both current.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch report (2004) on the extension of Sharia to criminal law in Nigeria: Zamfara's governor was first, introducing the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999 (in force 27 January 2000), and by 2002 twelve northern states had adopted some form of Sharia into their criminal legislation - to date the only states where Sharia courts have jurisdiction to try criminal cases.

The UK Home Office's June 2025 country note carries Kaduna's own row in its twelve-state Sharia penalties table (section 8.4.3, ILGA-derived): Kaduna's Sharia Penal Code Law (2002) with death by stoning as the maximum for liwat (sodomy) and same-sex acts between women punishable 'at the discretion of the qadi (Sharia court judge)'. Section 3.1.6 and 8.2.19 add that Kaduna separately adopted its own secular Penal Code in 2017, whose Section 259 punishes 'unnatural offences' - sodomy, lesbianism, bestiality - with up to 21 years' imprisonment and a fine, above the federal 14-year ceiling. Dated government confirmation of the two-layer criminalisation this record claims: a harsher Kaduna-specific secular statute plus a parallel Sharia layer applying to Muslims.

Ostien's annotated volume lists Kaduna's Sharia Penal Code Law 2002, Law No. 4 of 2002, signed into law and coming into operation on 21 June 2002 (Kaduna State Gazette No. 17 Vol. 36, 4 July 2002, pp. A15-A108, bound with the Sharia Criminal Procedure Code), and its annotation records that Kaduna is one of only three states whose enacted text states 'Whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm)' - with no unmarried/married graduation - while the lesbianism offence is left to ta'azir (discretionary punishment). Enactment-level evidence that Kaduna's Sharia layer is its own promulgated parallel criminal code carrying the bloc's capital ceiling for men's same-sex acts, confirming this record's stacked-architecture finding without relying on umbrella coverage.

records.name: Katsina
records.current_summary: Katsina is one of the twelve northern Nigerian states that built a parallel Sharia criminal jurisdiction over Muslims in the 1999–2002 wave, documented in an international-rights organisation's chapter on the extension and in a June 2025 government country-of-origin note on the country's hybrid legal system. Its code stands out for reach: the same 2025 note records Katsina as one of only two states whose law carries the death penalty as the maximum for same-sex acts between women as well as men.  No court-case study samples Katsina, no Hisbah operation is documented for it, and no trans-specific incident is on record; the elevated statutory reach over women's conduct is the differentiating fact, with the bloc-wide caveat that enforcement data are partial.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (2004) 'Nigeria: Unconsensual Sodomy Laws' chapter, fetched fresh this wave: documents the wave of Sharia adoption across northern Nigeria, explicitly listing the twelve states concerned — Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe, Zamfara — and tracing it from Zamfara's Shari'a Establishment Law (promulgated 27 Oct 1999, in force 27 Jan 2000). Serves this record's northern-bloc criminalisation claim; freshness confirms the provisions still in force.

UK Home Office Country Policy and Information Note, 'Nigeria: Sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics' (version 4.0, June 2025): documents the hybrid legal system and the 12-state Sharia criminal layer, its coverage of women, and arrest-data limits. (Cache captured the front-matter only; content as catalogued in the research dossier.)

Ostien's annotated volume lists Katsina's Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, Law No. 2 of 2001, coming into operation on 20 June 2001 and gazetted in Katsina State Gazette Vol. 12 No. 23, 27 August 2001, and its annotation records Katsina among the three states (with Kaduna and Kebbi) whose sodomy text reads 'Whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm)', while the lesbianism offence is punished by stoning to death - footnote 183 shows only Kano and Katsina reaching that capital maximum, against the harmonised code's base of 50 lashes and up to six months. Independent academic source for this record's claim that Katsina is one of only two states whose law carries death as the maximum for same-sex acts between women as well as men.

records.name: Kebbi
records.current_summary: Kebbi runs Sharia criminal law as one of the twelve northern states that had adopted it by 2002, with Sharia courts exercising criminal jurisdiction over Muslim defendants in parallel with the federal system (Human Rights Watch, 2004). The federal penal code criminalises same-sex conduct nationwide, and the UK Home Office country note (June 2025) records that these twelve states' Sharia penal codes extend that criminalisation to same-sex acts between women, with a maximum of death for men and flogging or imprisonment for women.  No Kebbi-specific enforcement record against trans people exists; the case-level documentation of Sharia enforcement covers three other bloc states (USCIRF study, 2017). For a Muslim or perceived-Muslim trans visitor who is outed, the practical difference from the rest of the country is jurisdictional: exposure to a Sharia court applying a criminal code that is broader in scope and harsher in penalty than the federal statute alone.

sources.claim: HRW 2004 report, chapter IV 'The extension of Shari'a to criminal law': Zamfara first re-adopted criminal Shari'a (Shari'a Establishment Law enacted 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000); by 2002 twelve northern states - Kebbi among them - had Shari'a criminal legislation and Sharia courts with criminal jurisdiction over Muslims, the only states with such jurisdiction.

The UK Home Office's June 2025 country note carries Kebbi's own row in its twelve-state Sharia penalties table (section 8.4.3): Kebbi's Penal Code (Amendment) Law (Law No. 21) (2000) with death by stoning for liwat (sodomy) and up to 50 lashes with imprisonment for up to 6 months for same-sex acts between women - the standard bloc penalty for women's conduct rather than the Kano/Katsina capital maximum. Dated government confirmation that Kebbi's Sharia layer extends criminalisation to acts between women, matching this record's claim that the state's code is broader in scope and harsher than the federal statute for Muslim defendants.

Ostien's annotated volume lists Kebbi's Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000, Law No. 21 of 2000, signed into law and coming into operation on 1 December 2000 (Kebbi State Gazette Vol. 2 No. 1, Supplement, 31 December 2000), and its annotations record Kebbi as one of three states (with Kaduna and Katsina) whose enacted text states 'Whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm)', while lesbianism follows the harmonised code's 50 lashes and up to six months' imprisonment. Enactment-level confirmation that Kebbi adopted its own Sharia penal layer in the 1999-2002 wave with a capital ceiling for men's acts and women's same-sex conduct criminalised, grounding this record's jurisdictional-difference finding in Kebbi's own statute.

records.name: Niger
records.current_summary: Niger State operates Sharia criminal law as part of the twelve-state northern bloc adopted by 2002, with Sharia courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslim defendants (Human Rights Watch, 2004). The federal anti-discrimination statute criminalises same-sex conduct nationwide; the UK Home Office country note (June 2025) records that the Sharia layer in these states extends criminalisation to acts between women.  No Kebbi-style state-specific enforcement or Hisbah record against trans people is documented for Niger; case-level enforcement records exist for other bloc states. The Sharia system adds a parallel criminal jurisdiction that the federation's southern states do not have, under which an outed Muslim or perceived-Muslim trans visitor faces broader charges and harsher penalties than under federal law alone.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (2004) 'Nigeria: Unconsensual Sodomy Laws' chapter, fetched fresh this wave: documents the wave of Sharia adoption across northern Nigeria, explicitly listing the twelve states concerned — Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe, Zamfara — and tracing it from Zamfara's Shari'a Establishment Law (promulgated 27 Oct 1999, in force 27 Jan 2000). Serves this record's northern-bloc criminalisation claim; freshness confirms the provisions still in force.

UK Home Office Country Policy and Information Note, 'Nigeria: Sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics' (version 4.0, June 2025): documents the hybrid legal system and the 12-state Sharia criminal layer, its coverage of women, and arrest-data limits. (Cache captured the front-matter only; content as catalogued in the research dossier.)

Ostien's sourcebook reproduces Niger State's own Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000 in full — a law to amend Penal Code Law Cap 94, Laws of Niger State, to review the punishments therein, gazetted in the Niger State of Nigeria Gazette No. 8, Vol. 25 of 9 March 2000 (pp. B29-B36) and coming into force on 4 May 2000. The enactment defines 'adultery' to include sodomy and inserts section 68A, under which a Muslim convicted of a listed offence and proved against him to the Islamic evidentiary standard receives the harsher Sharia-specified punishment (with amputation added to the caning paragraph of section 68), while the ordinary Penal Code punishment otherwise applies. State-level statutory proof that Niger, like the other northern bloc states, built a distinct criminal track for Muslim defendants — the legal layer this record identifies as the visitor-facing risk beyond federal law.

The annotated sourcebook catalogue records Niger: Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000, HB.4/2000, signed into law on 22 February 2000 and coming into operation on 4 May 2000 (Niger State Gazette Vol. 25 No. 8, 9 March 2000). The editor notes it is not a complete Sharia Penal Code: it merely amends the Penal Code of 1960 so that certain sections, applied to Muslims, carry different burdens of proof and different punishments than when applied to non-Muslims, and it is printed in its entirety in Part IV of the same chapter. Confirms the state-specific enactment behind this record's claim that an outed Muslim visitor in Niger State stands under a harsher parallel legal frame than federal law alone.

flags: the penal code extends criminalisation to same-sex acts between women

freshness.fact: Niger state is within the 12 northern sharia-penal-code states criminalising same-sex acts (death maximum for men); federal/state strands also criminalise; current per CPIN.

records.name: Imo
records.current_summary: Imo combines community violence with active state policing against gay people. In April 2018 a crowd in Isiala Mbano stripped two men accused of gay sex, beat them and paraded them through the streets with palm leaves tied around them; a follow-up report records that police took the two men in custody. In February 2025 the state police command announced it had stormed a 'same-sex party' at a hotel in Owerri, arresting eight suspects and charging them under the 2014 anti-homosexuality law, citing its 14-year term — the command's briefing expressly framed the enforcement as covering a 'gay, lesbian, bisexual and/or transgender act'.  The pattern runs across years and across modalities: mob justice met without accountability in 2018, and named, state-command enforcement invoking the criminal law in 2025. For a discovered visitor here, risk comes from neighbours and police alike.

sources.claim: 76crimes (26 Apr 2018): two men in Imo State were stripped, beaten and paraded through the streets accused of gay sex; a NoStringsNG inquiry found the victims were themselves arrested by police and may need legal support. Documents community vigilantism plus police processing of the accused.

Nigerian Newspoint (19 Feb 2025): Imo Police Command foiled a same-sex party at Graziella Hotels, Orogwe (Owerri West), arrested many gay and lesbian suspects, with fleeing attendees on a police search list. Evidence of active 2025 police enforcement against same-sex gatherings in Imo.

records.name: Edo
records.current_summary: In May 2018 in Ekpoma, a community discovered two men having sex; one was lynched to death and the other escaped. The coverage framed the act as an 'abominable' one defying 'the traditional laws and heritage of the land', and no prosecution is recorded: customary moral judgement operating lethally, with complete impunity. For national context, a rights-monitoring report published in January 2025 documented 556 violations against real or perceived LGBT people affecting 850 victims across Nigeria in 2024 — and states these are only a fraction of the true scale.  Edo's finding is the Ekpoma killing itself: where a discovered visitor can face lethal 'community justice' invoked in the name of tradition, answered afterwards by nobody.

sources.claim: Nigerian Observer (May 2018): in Ekpoma a mob lynched one of two men caught together and the other escaped, framed as an 'abominable act' under traditional heritage. Documents fatal community violence in Edo State.

The Initiative for Equal Rights (TIERs) '2024 Human Rights Violations Report' (published January 2025): annual documentation of violations based on real or perceived SOGIESC in Nigeria; per the dossier, its 2024 edition records 556 violations affecting 850 victims across the reporting period and states these represent only a fraction of the true scale.

On 10 June 2010 The Nigerian Observer reported from Benin City (Oredo LGA, Edo State) that a middle-aged man, Mark Osato Edomwonyi, narrowly escaped being killed by a mob after he was caught in a same-sex act with his partner Paddy in Paddy's rented apartment; a neighbour raised the alarm and Mark fled through the backyard before the mob arrived, which then 'unleashed terror' on Paddy. No police intervention, arrest or prosecution is recorded in the report, and Mark's whereabouts were still unknown at filing. First incident-level evidence for Edo beyond the 2018 Ekpoma killing: lethal mob 'community justice' operates in the state capital too, with no documented law-enforcement response.

The Nigerian Observer reported on 15 August 2008 that police declared Ugbogbo Ovbukhan wanted over 'gay practice' after he and his partner Jerry were caught in the act in a remote community in Edo State in February 2008; a mob mercilessly beat the two for desecrating the community, Ovbukhan escaped before police arrived, and the police arrested Jerry for interrogation. Direct evidence that Edo's police machinery pursued same-sex couples on the ground in 2008 — a community lynching attempt answered by arrest and a wanted declaration rather than protection.

flags: The dossier groups Edo with Imo as the 'non-Sharia southeast/west belt' where violent community justice substitutes for formal enforcement

records.name: Aceh
records.current_summary: Aceh is the only province in this country operating a codified religious criminal law of its own: the Qanun on jinayat (No. 6/2014) criminalises same-sex conduct (liwath, musahaqah) and close proximity (khalwat), with public caning as its signature punishment, applied by Islamic Shariah courts and policed by the Wilayatul Hisbah religious force alongside the secular Satpol PP units. Enforcement is active and widening: in August 2025 a Sharia court — sitting behind closed doors — sentenced two men to 80 strokes each for hugging and kissing, caned in a public park before around 100 spectators, with eight more people caned the same day; up to 100 strokes are available for morality offences generally, and Amnesty International called the practice 'state-sanctioned discrimination and cruelty'.  The Qanun does not name transgender people, but enforcement reaches them: a February 2025 boarding-house round-up detained a waria and a gay student facing up to 100 strokes under the liwath provision, with officials urging landlords to police tenants; in January 2018 police detained twelve transwomen and shaved their heads to teach them 'how to act like real men'. Private consensual conduct that carries no criminal penalty in any other province here can be publicly caned by a court in Aceh.

sources.claim: QURU: Journal of Family Law and Culture (doi 10.59698/quru.v3i1.405): 'The Increasing Number of Waria in Banda Aceh: Between Social Challenges and Law Enforcement' by UIN Ar-Raniry scholars (keywords: Law Enforcement, Waria, Aceh, Islamic Law, Qanun). Aceh legal scholarship analysing the rise of waria cases through a sharia-law-enforcement lens — the academic counterpart to the record's enforcement claims.

CBS News/AP (26 Aug 2025): two men were publicly caned in conservative Aceh province after a sharia court convicted them of hugging and kissing — the documented Aug-2025 caning episode the record's summary is built on, confirming public caning as the province's signature punishment.

iNews Aceh (undated local report, Feb-2025 round-up context): Satpol PP and Wilayatul Hisbah Banda Aceh secured an alleged gay couple in a boarding house; a local advocate urged police to investigate and boarding-house owners to monitor tenants. Supports the record's Feb-2025 enforcement-reaches-trans-people claim.

UNSW Human Rights Research Centre: transgender women face the highest rates of violence among LGBTIQ Indonesians, with survey data on relative social hostility; underpins this record's Indonesia-wide trans-violence context including the Jan-2018 twelve-transwomen detention claim that no Aceh-specific source in this record covers (rule-5 keep).

records.name: KwaZulu-Natal
records.current_summary: KwaZulu-Natal is where documented street violence against queer people meets the country's most powerful traditional authority. A 2024 criminology study from a university in the province documents queerphobic violence and victimisation of self-identifying queer sexual minorities in KwaMashu, a township north of Durban — daily life in which the constitutional guarantee of equality does not reach. In January 2012 the Zulu King's anti-gay remarks at a harvest festival made the collision explicit: the royal house insisted the reported 'rotten' wording was a mistranslation; the South African Human Rights Commission said it would investigate; the provincial premier backed the royal family; and the Congress of Traditional Leaders of South Africa (CONTRALESA) responded that the Pietermaritzburg gay and lesbian network demanding an apology had shown the king 'disrespect' and was 'only seeking fame'.  For a discovered visitor, the province's pattern is that local moral authority — monarchy, chiefly councils, and the provincial government siding with them — has publicly ranged against queer claims, while academic documentation shows queerphobic violence persisting in its townships.

sources.claim: University of KwaZulu-Natal (Durban) Masters criminology thesis, 2024 (Buthelezi, Ayanda Nomfundo): 'A criminological exploration of queerphobic violence and victimisation of self-identifying queer sexual minority in KwaMashu Township' — 15 queer participants purposively sampled from the Imvelo Yesizwe Organisation, in-depth interviews; findings report significant victimisation of queer individuals in township settings and examine adequacy of support/interventions and safety strategies.

PinkNews (26 Jan 2012): Zulu King Goodwill Zwelithini's anti-gay remarks at a harvest festival prompted demands for apology; police opened investigation, with the KwaZulu-Natal Premier and Contralesa weighing in on the royal family's account. Region-specific evidence of top traditional authority hostility toward gay people in the province.
